title: Safeguarding Children and Young People Policy
summary: How we protect children and young people under 18 whom our staff meet while caring for adults in their homes: the boundaries staff keep with children, asking about children and young carers at assessment, recognising harm, reporting and referring to children's social care, female genital mutilation, allegations against staff involving children, and information sharing. It applies to everyone who works for us.

keyPoints.intro: We care for adults, but our staff often meet children in the homes we visit. If anything you see, hear or are told worries you about a child, you must report it in the same way as a concern about an adult.
points: If a child is in immediate danger, seriously hurt or a crime is happening, call 999 first, then phone the office or the On-call Manager.
Report anything that worries you about any child you meet or hear about through work, including domestic abuse in a home where a child lives or stays; you do not need proof.
Phone the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, before you leave the visit and speak to a person; if nobody answers within 15 minutes, phone the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager directly.
If a child tells you something, listen calmly, do not ask leading questions, never promise to keep it secret, and never confront or warn a parent or anyone else; note the child's exact words.
Report it in the CareFlow app as a Safeguarding Concern incident before your shift ends; never examine or photograph a child, and describe in words anything you saw.
Never give a child personal care or medicines, babysit or look after a child, give a child a lift, stay alone with a child behind a closed door or bring any child to a visit, even if a parent asks.

The only exception is an emergency: if a child would otherwise be alone or unsafe, stay with them, phone the office and wait until a responsible adult, the police or children's social care takes over; the office covers your next visits.
Never give a child your phone number, a key or a key safe code, contact them by phone, text or social media, give them gifts or money, or take their photograph.

Tell the office the same day about any change in who lives in or visits the home, and if a child seems to be caring for the person, such as helping with washing, toileting, medicines or lifting; never leave a care task for a child.
Report at once to the Registered Manager any concern that a colleague has harmed a child or may be a risk to children, at work or outside it.
Tell the Registered Manager or HR Manager before your next shift if the police or children's social care start investigating your own conduct towards a child.

If you are a registered nurse, social worker or similar professional and a girl under 18 tells you she has had FGM or you see signs of it, you must personally phone the police on 101 by the end of the next working day.

blocks.p: {{organisation}} provides care to adults in their own homes. We do not care for children, but our staff meet them every day: the children and grandchildren of the people we support, young carers, and children who live with or visit the person. Our staff may be the first to notice that a child is being harmed or is caring for a parent without help.

{{organisation}} will never ignore a child at risk because the child is not the person we care for. Everyone who works for us reports any concern about a child as urgently as one about an adult. Because our staff are checked for work with adults, not children, we keep firm boundaries with children.

This policy makes sure that every concern about a child reaches the right agency on time, young carers get support, staff never take on the care of children, and allegations against staff involving children reach the Local Authority Designated Officer within one working day.

This policy applies to everyone who works for us, wherever they work, including on call and online. It covers every child (anyone under 18) we meet or hear about through our work, unborn children where there is concern for their safety after birth, and any member of our staff under 18.

A concern about anyone aged 18 or over, including a young person still receiving children's services, is handled under the Safeguarding Adults Policy and the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure, which this policy builds on. The staff side of allegations is in the Managing Allegations Against Staff Procedure, domestic abuse in the Domestic Abuse Policy, radicalisation in the Prevent and Radicalisation Guideline, and employing under-18s in the Young Workers Procedure.

rows: Child
Anyone who has not yet reached their 18th birthday. We say "young person" for 16 and 17-year-olds, who are still children in law.
Significant harm
The threshold at which the local authority must make enquiries under section 47 of the Children Act 1989; it can come from one serious event or a build-up of smaller concerns.
Children's social care front door
The local authority's single point for child safeguarding referrals and advice, with an emergency duty team out of hours.
Young carer
A person under 18 who provides or intends to provide care for another person (Children Act 1989, section 17ZA).
Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO)
The local authority officer who manages allegations against people who work with children.
Local safeguarding children partnership
The arrangements made in each area by the local authority, integrated care board and police, whose procedures, thresholds and escalation route we follow.
FGM
Female genital mutilation: any procedure that removes or injures the female external genitalia for non-medical reasons. It is a crime in the UK.

blocks.p: The Directors are accountable for safeguarding children across {{organisation}} and never accept a contract or care package that would require our staff to care for or supervise a child. The Nominated Individual is the board-level lead for safeguarding children and acts as safeguarding lead if the Registered Manager and Deputy Manager are both unavailable.

The Registered Manager is our designated safeguarding lead for children as well as adults and takes the lead's decisions in this policy. They keep the children's social care front door, emergency duty team and LADO details for every area we work in on the Local Safeguarding Contacts sheet.

The Deputy Manager acts as safeguarding lead when the Registered Manager is absent or conflicted. Out of hours, the On-call Manager takes the lead's immediate actions and hands over to the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager by 10am on the next working day.

subsections.heading: Care Coordinators and Field Care Supervisors

blocks.p: As assessors they record the children and young carers in each household. Care Coordinators make sure no care plan relies on a child, act on young carers, and with Office staff rearrange a care worker's next visits when the care worker stays with a child or waits for advice. Field Care Supervisors, and Senior Care Workers authorised as supervisors, test child safeguarding knowledge at supervision, including the yearly child scenario.

subsections.heading: Care Workers, Senior Care Workers, Office staff and HR Manager

blocks.p: Care Workers and Senior Care Workers keep the boundaries in this policy and report and record every concern; working alone, they get advice by phone from the office in office hours or the On-call Manager out of hours. Office staff record any concern phoned in, in the caller's words, and pass it to a manager at once. The HR Manager manages the staff side of allegations and keeps a list of staff whose professional registration brings the FGM reporting duty.

{{organisation}} provides personal care to adults aged 18 and over only, as our statement of purpose sets out, and carries out no regulated activity relating to children. Our staff hold enhanced DBS checks for the adult workforce with a check of the adults' barred list; they are not checked against the children's barred list.

rows: Children Act 1989, section 47
The local authority must make enquiries when it has reasonable cause to suspect that a child in its area is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm.
We refer; children's social care decides whether the threshold is met. Our staff never investigate.
Working together to safeguard children 2026

Statutory guidance: anyone with a concern about a child should refer it, not assume someone else will, and immediately where a child may be suffering significant harm; adult services should ask whether there are children in the family, including any pregnancy.
We follow it and each local safeguarding children partnership's procedures.
Duty to report

Apart from the FGM duty below, no law in England yet requires a care worker to report suspected child abuse. The Crime and Policing Act 2026 duty to report suspected child sex offences (section 85) was not in force on 5 November 2026 and covers activities with children, not adult home care.
Our policy makes reporting every concern about a child mandatory.
Domestic Abuse Act 2021, section 3
A child who sees or hears, or experiences the effects of, domestic abuse, and is related to the victim or the abuser, is a victim of domestic abuse in their own right.
We always report domestic abuse in a household where a child lives or regularly stays.
Care Quality Commission (Registration) Regulations 2009, regulation 18

We must notify CQC without delay of any abuse or allegation of abuse in relation to a person we support, and of any incident reported to or investigated by the police, that occurs while we provide care or as a consequence of it.

The Registered Manager notifies under the Statutory Notifications to CQC Procedure, including a police incident involving a child and (our policy) any allegation that a person we support has abused a child, without delay and within 24 hours of the referral or police report.

blocks.p: The children's information sharing duty in section 16LA of the Children Act 2004, in force since 30 September 2026, falls on the bodies listed in section 11 of that Act, such as local authorities, the NHS and the police, and on providers they commission for their functions for children, not on adult home care commissioned under the Care Act 2014. If children's services ever commission care from us, such as support for a parent, the safeguarding lead shares information for that package as the duty requires.

sections.heading: Children in the homes we visit

blocks.p: At every initial assessment and care plan review, the assessor asks about and records, in the initial assessment and the People involved part of the care plan: each child who lives in, stays at or regularly visits the home (first name, age and relationship); any pregnancy in the household; any child who helps with the person's care; the adult who will look after any child in the person's care if the person is suddenly taken ill or admitted to hospital, and how to reach them; any social worker or child protection plan for a child, as far as the family wishes to say; and anyone in or visiting the home known to pose a risk to children. Care workers tell the office the same day of any change in the household, and the Care Coordinator updates the care plan within 7 days. A known risk to children goes into the person's risk assessments and the care team is briefed before their next visit.
Staff are friendly to children but are never responsible for them. Staff must never:

bullets: give a child personal care or medicines, or feed, dress, bath or change a child;
look after, supervise or babysit a child, or agree to be left in charge of one, even for a few minutes;
take a child out, give a child a lift, or collect a child from school or nursery;
take a child into a room alone or stay alone with a child behind a closed door;
give a child their phone number, a key or a key safe code, contact a child by phone, text or social media, give a child gifts or money, or photograph a child;
bring their own or any other child to a visit.

blocks.p: If a parent asks for any of these, the care worker politely declines and tells the office the same day. Staff ask children to leave the room during personal care, for the person's dignity.

The only exception is an emergency: if a child would otherwise be alone or unsafe, for example because the parent we support has collapsed, the care worker stays with the child until a responsible adult, the police or children's social care takes over, and phones the office or On-call Manager. The office or On-call Manager contacts the adult named in the care plan or other family, calls the police or the emergency duty team if no responsible adult can arrive within 1 hour, and covers the care worker's next visits; the waiting time is paid working time.

If the person we support does not answer the door and only a child is at home, the care worker follows the No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure and tells the office a child is there; if the child would otherwise be alone, the office acts as in the emergency exception above. The care worker does not go in to wait or search with the child unless the child says the person is hurt or unwell inside: then they call 999 and go in to help.

An adult may be eligible for care to help them look after a child. Where commissioned care includes this, the care plan states exactly what our staff do to help the parent, who stays present and in charge of the child throughout. For example, a care worker may prepare a child's meal for the parent to give, but never feeds the child. The Registered Manager approves every such care plan before it starts.
Local authorities must consider any child involved in caring for an adult they assess, and must assess a young carer who may need support. We make sure they know.

steps: The care worker or assessor tells the office the same day if a child seems to be providing care, especially personal care, medicines, moving and handling, care at night or care that keeps the child from school.
The Care Coordinator records it in the care plan and talks to the person, and the young carer's parent if different, about asking for support.

Within 2 working days, the Care Coordinator writes to the local authority or commissioner asking for the person's care to be reviewed and for a young carer's needs assessment; a self-funding family is helped to make the request.

If the person objects, the safeguarding lead decides whether the child's welfare requires sharing anyway, recording the reasons, and refers to children's social care if the child may be suffering significant harm.

blocks.p: No care plan relies on a child to carry out a care task, let us into the home, cover a late or missed visit, act as interpreter or be the person's chosen contact for missed visits.

We do not accept referrals to care for anyone under 18, and care starts no earlier than the 18th birthday; before then the Registered Manager, Deputy Manager or a Care Coordinator may meet the young person to plan their care, always with a parent or the young person's social worker present. Nobody under 18 works in a care role or goes on visits for us, including students and work experience. A concern that a member of staff under 18 is being harmed is handled under this policy, and an allegation that a colleague has harmed them goes to the LADO.
A sign is not proof; it is a reason to report. Staff report what they see and hear and the safeguarding lead decides what it means.

columns: Signs staff may notice in the home
rows: Physical abuse
Injuries the explanation does not fit; any injury to a baby who is not yet mobile; a child who flinches or is afraid to go home.
Emotional abuse
A child constantly shouted at, belittled, threatened or ignored; a very withdrawn or anxious child.
Sexual abuse
Sexual language or behaviour unusual for the child's age; sexual images on view; a child who talks about a secret with an adult.
Neglect
A child often hungry, dirty or poorly dressed; no safe sleeping place for a baby; young children left with an adult who cannot look after them; a child often at home during school hours.
Exploitation and online harm

Unexplained money, phones or gifts; unknown older 'friends'; a child who goes missing; the home of the person we support taken over for drugs or crime (cuckooing); a child secretive or distressed about online contacts.
Honour-based abuse, forced marriage and FGM
A girl who talks about a special ceremony or long trip abroad; a young person fearful of a planned marriage.

blocks.p: Most parents with care needs look after their children well, but risk rises where illness, mental ill-health, alcohol or drug use, or a violent or controlling relationship leaves a child's needs unmet. Staff always report:

bullets: domestic abuse in any household where a child lives or regularly stays;
a pregnancy where there are concerns for the baby after birth;
a young carer who is doing too much or whose schooling or health is suffering;
any adult, including the person we support, who has harmed a child or is known to pose a risk to children and has contact with them;
images of child sexual abuse on any device, which staff never touch, copy or forward;
a child under 16 (under 18 if disabled) apparently living for 28 days or more with someone who is not a parent or close relative (possible private fostering).

blocks.p: When an adult we support says they were abused as a child, we listen and offer support. If the abuser may still have contact with children, the safeguarding lead tells the police, even without the adult's agreement, recording the reasons.

sections.heading: Responding to a concern about a child

steps: If a child is in immediate danger, seriously hurt or unwell, or a crime is happening, call 999. If you feel threatened, leave and phone from somewhere safe.

If a child tells you something, listen calmly and ask only open questions such as "Is there anything else you want to tell me?". Never promise to keep a secret; explain that you must tell someone whose job is to keep them safe.
Do not investigate, examine or photograph the child, any injury or the home, and never confront or warn a parent or anyone else who may be responsible.

Phone the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, before you leave the visit, from outside the home, such as your car, if anyone who may be responsible could overhear. Give the child's name, age and address if known, what you saw, heard or were told, and who may be responsible. The office tells you whether to stay or go on, and tells your next person if you will be late. With no signal, or if your double-up colleague may be responsible, follow the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure.

If nobody answers within 15 minutes, phone the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager directly; if you still cannot reach a manager and the child is at risk, contact children's social care or the police yourself using your Local Safeguarding Contacts sheet.

Report the concern in the CareFlow app as a Safeguarding Concern incident before the end of your shift, with the child's exact words in quotation marks. In the daily visit notes, write only that a concern has been reported.

blocks.p: Within 1 hour of the report, the safeguarding lead or On-call Manager speaks to the person who raised the concern, checks earlier records about the household, and records whether the child is safe now, who may be responsible, whether a crime may have been committed and whether the adult we support is also at risk. Where there is reason to think a child is suffering or likely to suffer significant harm, the lead refers to children's social care, and to the police if a crime may have been committed. Where a family may need help but significant harm is not suspected, such as a struggling young carer, the lead sends a written request for help. If the adult we support is also at risk, the lead also refers under the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure.

If unsure, the lead asks the front door for advice the same day and records it. Every decision, including not to refer, is recorded with the reasons. A member of staff who disagrees may contact children's social care directly and will be supported in doing so.

The lead refers to the front door for the area where the child lives or, if the child is in danger elsewhere (for example visiting a grandparent we support), where the child is. The referral gives the child's name, age, address and school if known; the concern and the child's words; who may be responsible; what we know of the child's needs and the parents' ability to meet them; any immediate risk and action taken; and whether the parents know. The lead records the reference number and who took the referral.

The lead tells the parents about a referral unless that may put the child or anyone else at greater risk, a parent may be responsible, or children's social care or the police advise against it; where in doubt, the lead asks the front door first.

blocks.p: Working together to safeguard children expects children's social care to acknowledge a referral and decide on next steps within one working day, and to tell the referrer its decision. If there is no acknowledgement or decision by the end of the next working day, the lead phones to ask. If there is still no decision by the end of the third working day after the referral, or we believe a decision leaves a child at risk, the Registered Manager escalates in writing under the local safeguarding children partnership's escalation procedure, starting with the team manager, and tells the Nominated Individual. If the risk becomes immediate, the lead calls 999 or the emergency duty team.

When asked to a strategy discussion, child protection conference or child safeguarding practice review, the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager attends or sends a written report with a chronology by the date requested, and each action given to us is recorded with an owner and deadline. The adult we support keeps receiving care throughout.

The law requires anyone registered with a health or social work regulator, such as a nurse (Nursing and Midwifery Council), an occupational therapist (Health and Care Professions Council) or a social worker (Social Work England), who in the course of their work is told by a girl under 18 that she has had FGM, or sees physical signs that appear to show it, to notify the police for the area where she lives within one month. The duty is personal and cannot be passed to the safeguarding lead. It falls away only where the professional has reason to believe that another person registered with one of these health or social work regulators has already reported the same act; if unsure, they report.

Our policy, following Home Office best practice, is that the professional phones 101 by the end of the next working day, or 999 if the girl is at immediate risk, records the police reference number in the safeguarding record, and tells the safeguarding lead the same day; the lead refers to children's social care. Nobody examines a girl to look for signs of FGM.

Other staff report any FGM concern through the normal route. Where a girl may be at risk of FGM, the lead refers to children's social care and the police the same day, and at once if travel abroad is imminent. Where an adult woman we support says she has had FGM, the lead respects her wishes, offers support through her GP, and refers if a girl in her family may be at risk.

Any concern that a member of our staff, including a bank or agency worker, student or contractor, has harmed or may have harmed a child, may have committed an offence against or related to a child, or may pose a risk to children or be unsuitable to work with them, must be reported immediately to the Registered Manager. This includes conduct outside work, such as towards the worker's own children, because it may also put the adults we support at risk. A concern about a manager or Director is reported as the Safeguarding Adults Policy sets out.

steps: Within one working day, the Registered Manager informs the LADO for the area of the branch that employs the worker (and, if the child lives in another area, that area's LADO too) and, where a crime may have been committed, the police, and records the advice given.

The same day, the Registered Manager decides on a written risk assessment whether the worker is removed from particular visits or all care work, and tells a supplying agency. Removal is not a finding of guilt.
We interview nobody, start no internal investigation and tell the worker nothing about the allegation until the LADO and police agree.

The HR Manager manages the staff side under the Managing Allegations Against Staff Procedure; DBS and regulator referrals follow the Staff Fitness Concerns and DBS Referrals Procedure and the LADO's advice.
If an adult we support may also be at risk, the lead refers to adult safeguarding the same working day.

blocks.p: Staff must tell the Registered Manager or HR Manager before their next shift, and within 24 hours at most, if the police or children's social care begin investigating their own conduct towards a child. Failing to tell us is a disciplinary matter.

Worries about confidentiality must never stop a concern about a child being passed on. Staff tell the safeguarding lead everything; the lead shares only what children's social care, the police or the LADO need, by secure means, and records what was shared, with whom, when and why, including any decision not to share. The lead tells the family what has been shared, following the rule under Making the referral.

Under the Confidentiality and Information Sharing Policy, our lawful basis is the recognised legitimate interest of safeguarding a vulnerable individual, which includes anyone under 18 (UK GDPR, Article 6(1)(ea) and Annex 1, paragraphs 6 to 8). Health and other special category information is shared without consent under the Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 1, paragraph 18, where consent cannot be given or reasonably obtained or asking would prejudice the child's protection, with the appropriate policy document kept under the Data Protection Policy. Where it is safe to ask and the person concerned, or a parent for a young child, agrees, we share under UK GDPR, Article 9(2)(h), with the Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 1, paragraph 2 and section 11.

A concern about a child is recorded in a safeguarding record in CareFlow under the adult we support through whose care it arose, holding the child's details, the concern, decisions with reasons, information shared, referrals, reference numbers and outcome; access is restricted as for all safeguarding records. Body maps are never used for a child. Allegations against staff, and concerns about a member of staff under 18, are recorded in the staff record. Retention follows the Records Management and Retention Policy and the Safeguarding Adults Policy.

blocks.p: At least once every 12 months, the safeguarding scenario at each care worker's supervision is about a child, as the Supervision, Spot Checks and Appraisal Policy sets out; anyone who cannot say how they would report it is retrained before their next unsupervised visit. Every employee acknowledges this policy in CareFlow by the deadline in the Induction and Care Certificate Procedure and within 14 days of each new major version; a minor version does not need acknowledging again.

blocks.p: The annual safeguarding report to the Directors includes children: activity, outcomes, learning from our concerns and local child safeguarding practice reviews, and next year's actions. Every shortfall gets an action, owner and deadline in the service improvement plan.

This policy is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager, checked by the Nominated Individual and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy, and sooner after a change in law or guidance (including commencement of the duty to report suspected child sex offences), a change to local procedures, a serious incident involving a child, an inspection finding, or when monitoring shows the arrangements are not working.
